query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation is dominated by thermally activated segregation and precipitation of Cr-rich nitrides and σ phases along grain boundaries in Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, which embrittle the FCC matrix and significantly reduce ductility, leading to catastrophic failure under mechanical stress.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with a homogeneous, supersaturated FCC matrix and negligible pre-existing precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled heat treatments (annealing) within a narrow temperature window (approximately 900–1150 K) under both oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres to assess the role of environmental conditions on precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: Annealing at temperatures between 900 and 1150 K, where diffusion is sufficient to promote elemental segregation but low enough to avoid complete recrystallization; tests conducted under both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres to isolate kinetic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of fine Cr-rich nitrides and σ phase precipitates localized at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature exposure, especially under conditions that favor segregation, causes Cr and possibly other reactive elements to precipitate as nitride and σ phases. These precipitates concentrate at grain boundaries, reducing intergranular cohesion and ductility, thereby facilitating premature failure under applied stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built state, heat-treated samples will display a measurable increase in precipitate density at grain boundaries accompanied by reduced ductility and lower fracture strains in mechanical tests. Differences may also arise between oxidizing and reducing environments in terms of precipitation kinetics.
generation.baseline: The original as-manufactured microstructure with a supersaturated FCC matrix containing minimal precipitates.
generation.boundary: The precipitate-induced embrittlement mechanism becomes significant when annealing is performed between 900 and 1150 K; below this range diffusion is too slow, and above it, complete phase transformation may occur.
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of embrittling precipitates is expected, the exact role of the gas environment in modifying precipitation kinetics and the critical volume fraction of precipitates needed for marked embrittlement are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform heat treatments on samples at temperatures between 900 and 1150 K under both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Characterize precipitate density and distribution using TEM/SEM, then carry out mechanical tests (tensile or fracture toughness) to correlate precipitate formation with reductions in ductility.
measurements: Precipitate size, density, and location via microscopy
Comparative analysis between different gas atmospheres
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If heat-treated samples do not show a significant increase in grain-boundary precipitates or if the mechanical properties remain comparable to the baseline regardless of the annealing atmosphere, the hypothesis that degradation is driven by precipitate-induced embrittlement will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory CrMoNbWV HEA was obtained from elemental powders by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.The phase composition, microstructure, and properties of the manufactured alloy depended strongly on the sintering conditions. It was determined that in the MA-powder with a BCC solid solution structure, the Laves phases Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb precipitate under the SPS (41.6 vol.% at 1200 °C). Their volume fraction decreases when the SPS temperature increases and accounts for 21.5 vol.% at 1300 °C and 11.5 vol.% at 1400 °C. The presence of the oxides NbVO4–VO can be connected with the powder oxidation during the MA.The sintered samples exhibit the compressive strength of 2700–2870 MPa. The samples’ low plasticity is caused by the high volume fraction of the Laves phases localized at the grain boundaries. In the sample sintered at 1400 °C, the volume fraction of the Laves phases is lowered. However, the particle size of the oxides increases significantly. The coarse inclusions can serve as sources of crack initiation in the BCC-matrix.The synthesized CrMoNbWV HEA exhibited high corrosion resistance, hardness, and wear resistance. Unlike the classical Cantor alloys obtained by casting technology, the alloy obtained by SLM did not require prolonged exposure to high temperatures to produce secondary phase precipitation. SLM technology with Nitrogen protective atmosphere induced a fine secondary phases precipitation of nitrides and intermetallic phases in the as-built state. The cold-rolled plus annealed FCC matrix became unstable and secondary phases precipitated. The observed precipitation was made of tetragonal Cr-rich σ phase and of mixed Cr-(Fe, Mn, Co, Ni)-nitrides which nucleated at the triple points. The size of the σ phase precipitates increased with annealing temperature. When the annealing temperature was below the recrystallization temperature, the size of precipitates was small due to a low diffusion rate and confined at the grain boundaries of the as-built dendritic structure. When the temperature exceeded 1323 K, the σ phase dissolved and the alloy substantially returned to single phase with near equiatomic composition. σ phase and nitride precipitations yielded a significant alloy hardening only at room temperature and for annealing up to 923 K, that is, below recrystallization temperature.
